source.title: RAPO: Risk-Aware Preference Optimization for Generalizable Safe Reasoning
source.authors: Ze-Ming Wei; Qiao-Sheng Zhang; Xia Ben Hu; Xing-Cheng Xu

page_placements.theme: Explicit and intermediate safety reasoning can improve robustness

record.tranche_reason: The study measures harmful-prompt refusal and jailbreak success while examining safe-reasoning depth, and tests a different training method intended to adapt that depth to attack complexity. It does not measure the original fine-tuning intervention or token-position KL.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on safe-reasoning proportions and harmful-prompt ASR across attack sets, plus ASR after RAPO training and ablations. It does not test fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful or benign examples, aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant-prefix prefilling, suffix or decoding bypasses, or safety localization in weights. Values cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a defense-method paper for reasoning models. RAPO trains safe reasoning placed at the start of the thinking content, with length scaled to attack complexity, and reports its own jailbreak ASR against baselines. The only link to the claim is a citation of Qi et al. [25] calling alignment 'commonly superficial'. The study runs no harmful or benign fine-tuning attack (V1, V2) and measures no per-token KL or position-wise effect (V3). Its attacks are WildJailbreak-style prompts and PAIR/TAP rewrites, not prefilling, suffixes or decoding changes (V4). It does no parameter localization (V5) and no analysis of why alignment is shallow (V6). Its 'depth' means the length of safe-reasoning sentences in chain-of-thought, not safety spread across response token positions (V7). It never tests deepening against prefill or fine-tuning attacks. The safe-reasoning findings are a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue safe reasoning must scale in depth and length with attack complexity, with theory and correlational evidence. They report that RAPO beats SFT and RL baselines on jailbreak robustness while preserving utility.
record.recipe_differences: RAPO uses an SFT warm-up to format risk-adaptive safe reasoning, followed by GRPO with risk-aware and general reward signals. It is not the harmful/benign fine-tuning intervention or token-position KL measurement in the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model, attack dataset and complexity, and training recipe. The paper reports different outcomes for RAPO-SFT, harmful-only and benign-only data, and reward-component ablations.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen-3-1.7B, refusals contain a higher share of safe-reasoning sentences than successful jailbreaks across all five splits. The share falls as StrataSword complexity rises from L1 to L3 while ASR rises from 9% to 58%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In reasoning models, the amount of safety-related chain-of-thought predicts refusal and shrinks relative to attack complexity.

fits_no_version.finding: RL training that rewards safe reasoning scaled to prompt complexity cuts WildJailbreak ASR, for example from 68.7% to 5.6% on the DeepSeek distill, with MMLU-Pro roughly preserved.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Complexity-adaptive safe-reasoning training improves reasoning-model robustness to prompt-level jailbreaks.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated results. The safe-reasoning extraction uses sentence splitting and keyword matching, and the Table 5 ablation model is not identified. The reported association between safe-reasoning proportion and refusal does not by itself establish causality.
record.rows_left_out: The safe-reasoning token-count values in Table 1 are omitted because the recorded proportion and ASR rows capture the reported relation to outcomes. Table 4 baseline methods other than Base and RAPO are omitted; Table 7 baseline-method values are omitted while RAPO's adaptive-attack results are retained.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning attack on aligned models.
No benign fine-tuning attack measuring safety erosion.
No per-token KL or position-wise analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks; only prompt-level jailbreaks.
No analysis of the data or objective causing shallowness.
RAPO concentrates safe reasoning at the start of the thinking content. Spread across token positions and robustness to prefill or fine-tuning are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V7 link rests on a wording overlap: 'depth' here means chain-of-thought safe-reasoning length, not token-position depth. The ablation model in Table 5 is evidently Qwen-3-1.7B. The only engagement with the originals is the citation of Qi et al. as showing superficial alignment.

versions.untested_parts: Whether fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples makes safety-trained models comply.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning raises harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Whether compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes bypass safety.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether the data or training objective causes safety to be shallow.
The study trains adaptive safe reasoning and measures refusal/ASR, but does not test whether safety is distributed beyond the first response tokens or compare token-position distributions.

relation.reason: Section 2.1 cites Qi et al. [25] for superficial alignment. The study does not test or operationally use the specified shallow-alignment findings.

tranche.reason: The study measures safe-reasoning adequacy and its defense method's performance, without testing any listed claim version. Longer safety analysis at the beginning of thinking does not establish safety distributed beyond the opening tokens.

source_check.notes: R11–R22 are own-method benchmark comparisons, unsuitable as direct phenomenon evidence; versions=none and cannot_determine are appropriate. ASR uses the HarmBench classifier on both thinking content and final response.

statements.correction: Table 4: DeepSeek-distillation-qwen (1.5B), WildJailbreak ASR 68.7% Base → 5.6% RAPO; MMLU-Pro 31.2% Base → 30.3% RAPO. RAPO combines SFT warm-up with risk-aware GRPO.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: RAPO-trained models on the reported standard safety and jailbreak benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: RAPO is accompanied by lower ASR than the base models across the reported benchmarks; see R11-R22 and the full-recipe rows R25-R26.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Safe-reasoning and recipe ablations, and adaptive-attack evaluations
reader_labels.reason: SFT-only and benign-data-only results retain substantial WildJailbreak ASR; the adaptive-attack values have no base-model reference, and the study does not establish safety spread across response-token positions. See R23-R24, R29-R30, R35-R38.
